concepts.title: Organising Data with Tally Marks
concepts.definition: Raw information means little until it is organised: writing each observation and drawing tally strokes in fives beside it turns a jumble of numbers into a table that instantly shows how often each item occurs.
concepts.key_idea: Group tally strokes in fives - the fifth stroke cuts across - so counting becomes quick.
concepts.textbook_ref: hemh104.txt section 4.1 (looking for information, organising data)
question_patterns: organise the given raw data using tally marks
which item occurs most often in the collected data
how many observations belong to the given category
read the frequency of the given item from the tally table
prepare a table showing each entry and its count
what is the advantage of organising data before studying it

solution_steps.explain: Write each distinct item or value in a column.
Add one tally stroke for every occurrence, crossing the fifth over the first four.
Each five-group plus loose strokes gives the frequency.

concepts.title: Circle Graphs and Drawing Pie Charts
concepts.definition: A circle graph shows parts of a whole: each category's fraction of the total multiplied by 360 degrees gives the central angle of its sector, and drawing these sectors with a compass completes the pie chart.
concepts.key_idea: Fraction of the data times 360 degrees equals the slice angle.
concepts.textbook_ref: hemh104.txt section 4.2 (circle graph or pie chart, drawing pie charts)
question_patterns: draw a pie chart for the given data
find the central angle for the category that forms one third of the total
convert the given shares into angles for a circle graph
which sector is the largest in the given pie chart
verify that all sector angles add to 360 degrees
interpret the pie chart of the given survey

solution_steps.explain: Divide the category amount by the grand total.

concepts.title: Random Experiments and Equally Likely Outcomes
concepts.definition: In a random experiment like tossing a coin or throwing a die, the result is not fixed in advance; when no outcome is favoured over another - head or tail, any face of a die - the outcomes are equally likely, which is what lets us compute chances fairly.
concepts.key_idea: A fair experiment gives every outcome the same standing: heads and tails, all six faces alike.
concepts.textbook_ref: hemh104.txt sections 4.3.1-4.3.2 (getting a result, equally likely outcomes)
question_patterns: list all outcomes when a coin is tossed once
how many outcomes has throwing of a die
what are equally likely outcomes - define with an example
is getting a six on a fair die equally likely as getting a one
which experiments give equally likely outcomes
why is tossing a coin called a random experiment

solution_steps.explain: Write every possible result of the experiment before performing it.
No outcome should be special; each must carry the same chance.
Equally likely outcomes are exactly what probability needs.

concepts.title: Probability of an Event
concepts.definition: The probability of an event is the number of outcomes favouring it divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes - a value from 0 for the impossible to 1 for the sure event; the chance of a head in one toss is 1 out of 2.
concepts.key_idea: Favourable over total: 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, one half means a fair coin head.
concepts.textbook_ref: hemh104.txt sections 4.3.3-4.3.5 (linking chances to probability, events, real life)
question_patterns: find the probability of getting a head when a coin is tossed

numbers from 1 to 10 - find the probability of choosing a multiple of 3
can the probability of an event be more than 1 - justify

solution_steps.explain: List the outcomes that match the event.
Total equally likely outcomes sit in the denominator.
